newsitem.title: UK: Action man Simpson's reputation on line at GEC.
newsitem.headline: Action man Simpson's reputation on line at GEC.

text.p: George Simpson's reputation as the action man of British industry is on the line as he sets out to reshape General Electric Co Plc.
"It's like trying to wake up an elephant," says one ex-employee of the U.K. engineering group where, after 10 years of stagnation, investors are clamouring for change.
On Thursday, investors got a taste of Simpson's savvy when GEC and Finmeccanica SpA joined forces in a defence joint venture just one day after the British group announced a strategic review.
Simpson, the Scots accountant who cut his teeth at car-maker Rover before selling it to Germany's BMW, took over from veteran managing director Lord Weinstock last September.
Hopes are high that the experience and contacts he garnered while serving as deputy managing director at British Aerospace Plc could lead to an elusive merger with GEC.
Before joining GEC in September, Simpson's parting shot as boss of Lucas Industries was to merge it with Varity Corp of the U.S., giving LucasVarity Plc the critical mass to develop.

Simpson has wasted little time in stepping out of the shadow of his cautious predecessor Weinstock, announcing the defence deal with Finmeccanica of Italy in a deal which wraps together two billion pounds ($3.4 billion) of revenues.
The two sides will take cross-stakes in each others defence divisions, with the venture expected to be running within a year.
Analysts welcome the news as a notable first step and "a sign that Simpson is pushing through what he said he would," said Andy Crispin at SocGen.
The move comes the day after Simpson delivered his shake-up designed to shake GEC out of its strategic slumber.

Simpson offered a possible four billion pounds float of the 50-50 GEC-Alsthom rail and power joint venture, making its defence unit GEC-Marconi the new heart of the group through acquisitions and holding onto and repositioning its telecoms joint venture GPT.

Industry analysts said before the Finmeccanica/ GEC_Marconi deal was announced that the full impact of his gameplan is likely to be felt two to three years down the line and the jury was split on whether this was soon enough.
One analyst said after the review that the group had made "A promise of jam tomorrow -- a typical GEC story."
But others said it was unrealistic to expect mega-deals so soon, especially in the sensitive area of defence where political issues are entwined.

"My view is Simpson cannot change GEC in a day. You are not going to invest in GEC for a sharp increase in profits this year but for a return further down the line. In the long term the big deal will happen," said Sanjay Jha of Williams de Broe.
Finmeccanica is not the big deal investors are praying for. But the joint venture is a key stepping stone, said Crispin.

Simpson has also held out the possibility of some short-term shareholder value through the GEC-Alsthom flotation, with a decision in three months. If the float is agreed it could happen within the year.

The one billion pounds plus cash mountain (excluding joint venture cash) which Weinstock hoarded in his final years as chief will also be released and spent on acquisitions to bolster core sectors or possibly fund a share-buyback if no deals emerge.
The moves were bold by traditional GEC standards. But even with the flotation sweetener, some investors were left with the bitter taste of disappointment.
Looking ahead, it is clear that unless a major breakthrough defence deal emerges, the ability to create value in the short term is constrained.
Many of the strategic efforts -- apart from the Finmeccanica link-up -- remain no more than paper plans at this stage which left some investors still itchy for action and asking questions.
They wonder whether GEC can clinch a defence link-up which will catapult it into the kind of major league currently occupied by the U.S. defence industry giants after rapid consolidation.
The pressure is on following recent U.S. mega-mergers between Lockheed Martin Corp and Northrop Grumman Corp and Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas.

Analysts say GEC could afford to spend two billion pounds on defence deals and Simpson has said he is willing to gear up GEC if necessary. "The mere fact that I will now do that is a very significant change in GEC's policy," Simpson told Reuters.
He said he continued to talk to British Aerospace Plc . Another smaller deal could be the possible purchase of Siemens AG's defence arm.
Analysts and press commentators had whipped up a storm of speculation before the review announcement, building hopes of a defence wedding between GEC and Bae. But nothing happened.

The hoped-for asset swap with Siemens AG also failed to materialise. Analysts had speculated that GEC would trade its 60 percent stake in the telecoms joint venture GPT in return for Siemens' defence arm which is up for sale.

GEC-Marconi's most obvious defence partner is Thomson-CSF of France. But domestic political stumbling blocks have prevented the company being merged with a foreign firm. Marconi also partly matches up to the business of Alenia Difensa of Italy and Daimler-Benz Aerospace of Germany.

Williams de Broe's Jha believes the BAe deal would be best because "at least GEC would know it was merging with a company which is run efficiently and knows the meaning of value. It won't yield major cost savings but it will position it for bigger deals."
"At the end of the day shareholders want to know 'Will I get any money?' They don't care if they get it from a defence deal, a float or a buyback," Jha said. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
